content: Tinea capitis is a fungal infection that affects the scalp. It is also commonly referred to as ringworm of the scalp. Symptoms of Tinea Capitis: The infection may involve specific areas of the scalp or the entire scalp. Affected areas often appear bald with small black dots, which are the result of broken hair shafts. The skin in these areas may appear round, scaly, red, or swollen (inflamed). Pus-filled lesions, known as kerions, may develop. Some individuals may experience a low-grade fever, typically around 100–101°F. Swollen lymph nodes in the neck may also occur. Itching of the scalp is a common symptom. Causes of Tinea Capitis: Tinea capitis is caused by mold-like fungi known as dermatophytes. These fungi thrive in warm, moist environments. The infection is more likely to occur in individuals with: Minor injuries to the skin or scalp. Poor hygiene practices. Prolonged wetness of the skin, such as from excessive sweating. Risk Factors: Tinea capitis is highly contagious and can spread easily from person to person. It most commonly affects children and often resolves spontaneously at puberty, though it can occur at any age. The infection can be transmitted through direct contact with an infected person or by touching contaminated objects such as combs, hats, or clothing. Pets, particularly cats, can also spread the infection. Diagnosis: A healthcare provider may suspect tinea capitis based on the appearance of the scalp. A diagnostic tool called a Wood's lamp may be used to identify fungal infections of the scalp. A swab of the affected area may be sent for fungal culture, though results can take up to three weeks. In rare cases, a skin biopsy of the scalp may be performed. When to Seek Medical Attention: It is important to consult a healthcare provider if you experience symptoms of tinea capitis. Home remedies are not effective in treating this condition. Treatment: Oral antifungal medications, such as griseofulvin, terbinafine, or itraconazole, are prescribed to treat tinea capitis. These medications are typically taken for 4 to 8 weeks. Keeping the scalp clean is essential. Medicated shampoos containing ketoconazole or selenium sulfide may help slow or prevent the spread of the infection, but they are not sufficient to eliminate the fungus on their own. Family members and pets should be examined and treated if necessary. Adults should only use the shampoo if they show signs of infection. Washing towels in warm, soapy water and drying them after each use by an infected individual. Soaking combs and brushes in a solution of half bleach and half water for one hour daily for three days. Avoiding the sharing of personal items such as combs, hairbrushes, hats, towels, pillowcases, or helmets. Prognosis: Tinea capitis can be challenging to treat and may recur after treatment. In many cases, the condition resolves on its own during puberty. Possible Complications: Hair loss. Permanent scarring of the scalp. Development of pus-filled sores (kerions).
